cs.t: How much are you writing to those drives? Have you tried any drives that will extend their pseudo-SLC cache across the entire space, and then only partitioned 25-30% of the nameplate capacity?  That'll get you a terabyte for less than $300. Personally I've had two SSDs in active use and both have done a lot better than that.  One was MLC and died after 13 years, and the other is TLC and still working after 10 years.
cs.th: How Not to Buy a SSD

cs.t: We had a Samsung dishwasher. Took exactly 5 years for it to spill water to the floor. Now we have a Miele, as we do have their laundry machine and fridge already. The laundry machine is soon 20 years old, been doing laundry around 5-6 times every week and works still like new. The fridge is supposedly built by Liebherr. It feels really high quality: the door handle feels nice and locks the door properly. There are multiple different temperature areas that hold the temperature quite steady. The dishwashers have certain tiers. I don't know if it makes sense to pay for the TwinDos detergent system: you can wash dishes without filling detergent. The detergent is proprietary and quite expensive. Sadly if you want to connect the dishwasher to your home assistant, that feature is only in the most expensive models. The door that opens automatically when the program is done is great though. You can do the eco program which is quite slow, but it spends the last hours just the door open, and in the morning you have clean and dry dishes with minimal water and energy use.
cs.th: FreeMDU: Open-source Miele appliance diagnostic tools

cs.t: Buy a TV from 2016. Mine's a Samsung from 2016. It showed me a EULA on first boot. I declined it. It's been a dumb TV ever since. One input is a LibeELEC NUC, the other an Apple TV, because Netflix requires a botnet to stream >480p. 4K is unironically a meme. You don't need it. A set of decent floor standing speakers (and room treatment) will elevate your movie experience  far  more than more pixels ever will.

cs.t:
Sadly the Samsung TV I have was the best display for the price by a mile, so I've done what i can to balance usage and protection. Its connected to the wifi to allow for AirPlay natively.
The tv has a fixed IP at the router to block all traffic in and out of the network, and as a visibility layer its DNS'd through a PiHole too. Its unbelievably talkative over the network! In the 7 days just passed, its been 90% of the blocked requests by volume (there's no allowed domains from that IP). I'm still not convinced it isn't sneaking out data somehow - piggybacking off a connection somewhere to the neighbors TV. Its HDMI runs through a stereo amplifier, so it can't piggy-back off the connected PC that runs it. Maybe the PC (Mint) can run AirPlay somehow and I can disconnect it entirely from the internet? I feel overly paranoid about this device relative to everything else in the house, I'm not sure how justified that is.
cs.th: Ask HN: Which TV do you recommend for privacy?

cs.t: I shop for elite televisions at the “reuse” center, my latest score was a 2013 Panasonic plasma which is a perfectly good dumb TV hooked up to an XBOX ONE and a home theatre.  Downstairs I have a big curved Samsung 4K attached to my big PC.  Someday I’ll see the high end OLED that I crave. If you have the room and price is no object you definitely want at least 5.1 theatre,  both movies and TV programs sound great in 5.1. The next step up is a second subwoofer, even for music subwoofers take a load off your other speakers and reduce distortion.

cs.t: I allow my Samsung to connect to my local network, but then use openwrt and refuse to allow any outbound data from any IP using the MAC address of the television set. It cant update itself and no traffic suggests it can do anything regardless of what it might be collecting. Rooting it to prevent it from connecting to other wifi AP’s is probably the only better thing.
cs.th: Ask HN: Which TV do you recommend for privacy?

cs.t: First of all, open the TV and disconnect the wireless radio from the main board, on mine (Samsung) it was just unplugging one cable (AI or Google it).  I dislike doing stuff like that, but it was easy in my case, maybe you'll be lucky, too. Second, never use the "apps" built into the TV. Next, don't plug Ethernet into the TV.  Plug HDMI cables into the TV. Use a box of your choice on the other end of the HDMI cables.  This is now the box that you trust.  (Roku? Shield? Blu-ray? MacBook? PC? Linux? Playstation? XBox? Whatever you want.) The Smart TV itself is now fine.  Choose the devices you plug into it to play content.  The TV just shows it.
cs.th: Ask HN: Which TV do you recommend for privacy?

cs.t: I'm currently traveling with my spare laptop (a cheap old Samsung). I have Manjaro installed on it. I normally use a mac for work. But I don't like leaving 5K worth of laptop around in random hotels or airbnbs. I have about 30 years of experience with running Linux. Rarely as my main system (though I did use this particular laptop for a few months in between two macs at some point). I got rid of both snap and flatpak. I like the idea of those two. But they are just too much of a PITA to deal with. I'd like this stuff to work how it works on my mac: mount .app image, drag the app to the Applications folder and done. On Manjaro, if I want something, I just 'yay  ' it. I find it very telling how commercial application developers that actually do explicitly support Linux advertise their Linux support on their websites. Mostly it does not involve the words flatpak or snap. Just not a thing. Generally you'll find some link to a deb, rpm, or tar ball (in that order). And good luck with that. Yay does a fairly good job of converting deb files for use with arch based systems. It's how I installed Chat GPT Desktop on this thing before traveling, for example. Basically the status quo for commercial application developers targeting Linux is to: 1) ignore distros repackaging other people's software 2) ignore niche package management solutions 3) just cover the basics which is Ubuntu (deb) first and then everything else. Which means you get a deb file, maybe an rpm, and not much else typic…
cs.th: Flatpak – An Insecurity Nightmare

cs.t: Payments should be the obvious feature. The commercials for various smart watches show the same thing: somebody buying a coffee with just their watch. But the reality is different. On my smartwatch (an older Samsung, but same Google OS merged with Tizen) there's a PIN required if you enable payments on the watch. I understand why, the secure element requires it. But it makes every other feature of the watch useless to me. I don't have any secrets I want a watch to protect. I want to be able to time workouts while standing on a treadmill. They could solve this, only have large amounts require the code while letting me buy a coffee without it, but I'm sure there's some line in an agreement between Google and the banks prohibiting this. The risk has to be transferred to the customer, even if the likelyhood of somebody buying a coffee with my watch is low. Product design should consider all of these things, but getting out the next smartwatch without thinking it through is more inline with quarterly objectives. There isn't even a Steve around to piss off enough to do something about it.
cs.th: Pixel Watch 5

my common dumb test approach with fio     fio --rw=write --ioengine=sync --fdatasync=1 --directory=test-data --size=220m --bs=2300 --name=mytest
  
Consumer grade SSDs 100-500 iops, datacenter SSDs in thousands (like ~ 5 year old samsung model on Hetzher AFAIR had ~ 3000 iops in that test). Cheap VPSes  - easily in 5-30 iops of this sort more often then not, fsync/fdatasync is overlooked by programmers

cs.t: Technically the processor is on in low power mode, but the TV unit itself is not running. On pressing the power button, the interface does not appear immediately. First the screen displays the Samsung logo, then the system loads, then the (broadcast/HDMI/analog) TV signal appears several seconds later. I can hook up a power meter (if I can find it, unlikely), but if the system was fully running it would be near-instant like when you switch to your cable box that has a fan running 24/7 expelling hot air (in this case it would only have to turn on the screen itself). This is  about 3x longer than it takes my monitors of the same age to power on. (Samsung and Acer and Dell). I do not have the smart features enabled, not do I have it connected to any networks.
